text: Key persistent capability grants on package identity plus publisher rather than content hash so grants survive application updates, and revoke them on publisher change.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Write property-based and model-based tests for capability invariants (attenuation never widens authority, revocation is complete and observable, transfer preserves type) and evaluate Kani or a TLA+ model of the derivation core.
rationale: §9 rests entirely on these invariants holding and example-based tests cannot demonstrate absence of escalation paths.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Model debugger attachment, tracing of another component and reading another component's memory as explicit capabilities rather than same-user or root checks.
rationale: ptrace-style same-uid attach is the classic way ambient authority leaks between sandboxed applications.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the userspace capability representation (dense per-component handle-table index vs sparse unforgeable 64-bit token vs sealed-pointer layout reservable for CHERI) through an ADR backed by a prototype of each.
rationale: Handle representation is the most permanent ABI decision and determines whether hardware-assisted enforcement can ever be adopted without breaking binaries.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Prototype and benchmark capability revocation strategies (seL4-style derivation tree walk, indirection/epoch invalidation, lazy check-on-use) at 10^6 derived capabilities and choose one.
rationale: Revocation cost bounds how freely the OS can hand out attenuated capabilities, which is the entire security model.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the service discovery model (capability namespace object, broker component, or manifest-declared static wiring) by which a component obtains its initial and later capabilities.
rationale: Without a discovery decision every service invents its own bootstrap protocol and ambient authority creeps back in.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Research and decide how capabilities persist across component restart and reboot (sturdy references, revocable persistent grant store, or re-prompt), including which object types may ever be persisted.
rationale: A photo editor that loses access to every previously chosen file on relaunch is unusable, yet persistence weakens revocation guarantees.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Validate the frozen capability ABI on a CHERI emulator (QEMU-CHERI or Morello) as an explicit gate demonstrating that application-visible capability semantics survive hardware enforcement.
rationale: The baseline promises hardware-assist readiness; a concrete test prevents that promise from being an unverified assertion at 1.0.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Produce a machine-checked formal model (e.g. TLA+ or Alloy) of capability derivation, attenuation, transfer and revocation before the ABI freeze.
rationale: Security invariants that must hold for decades should be checked once formally rather than rediscovered through CVEs.

text: File descriptors are not the universal object abstraction; typed Capability<T> handles replace them natively.
Native applications must not receive ambient access to the user's machine.
Define and implement Capability<T> as the fundamental userspace reference to kernel objects.
ADR: replace file descriptors with typed capability handles; specify the handle table design.
ADR: ambient permissions are replaced by explicit capability grants; specify the grant sources (launcher, user choice, manifest).
Kernel Core owns capability enforcement as a native kernel responsibility.
Userspace receives Capability<T> handles rather than object pointers; implement the per-component capability table.
A capability must identify what object is referenced.
A capability must encode which operations the holder may perform (rights).
A capability must encode how the object may be transferred or delegated (transfer rights).
Capabilities must be unforgeable; userspace cannot mint a valid capability without the kernel.
Capabilities must be typed; using a Capability<File> where Capability<Channel> is expected must fail at the kernel boundary.
Capabilities must be transferable where permitted (send over channel, pass at component creation).
Capabilities must be revocable where appropriate; implement revocation that invalidates all derived capabilities.
Capabilities must be attenuable; implement derivation that only removes rights.
Capabilities must be inspectable; a holder can query type, rights and object identity of its own capabilities.
Capability<File, ReadWrite> may derive Capability<File, Read> but never Capability<File, Admin>; add a regression test for rights monotonicity.
ADR: rights representation (generic bitmask vs per-object-type typed rights vs rights as separate objects) including how Admin authority is expressed.
Resolve revocation semantics: eager vs lazy invalidation, revocation of in-flight operations, and cost bounds on revocation trees.
The capability design must not assume software-only enforcement; the ABI specification must reserve room for hardware-enforced capabilities.
Study CHERI-like capability pointers and document how Capability<T> would map onto them.
Study tagged memory architectures and their implications for MemoryObject and capability storage.
Study hardware provenance tracking and its fit with capability audit.
Application-visible capabilities must remain conceptually stable whether enforced by kernel metadata, page tables, CPU tags, hardware capabilities or combinations.
Define an enforcement-backend abstraction inside the kernel so capability checks can be implemented by kernel metadata today and hardware later.
Write a hardware-assisted capability readiness ADR listing the ABI invariants that must hold for future hardware enforcement.
No ambient authority: a native component starts with exactly the capabilities it was handed and nothing else.
A Component contains a Capabilities table.
Each component in a graph receives only the authority it requires; the graph description must be capability-explicit per component.
Persistent background execution beyond the lifetime of the owning application must require an explicit capability (e.g. Capability<BackgroundExecution>).
The object returned by the chooser must itself carry the authority (capability), so no path-based permission check follows selection.
Define persistent grants: how an application retains access to a user-selected object across restarts (durable capability, recent-files list) and how the user revokes it.
Capability representation must accommodate CHERI-style hardware capabilities (§8).
Study CHERI/Morello mapping of Capability<T> and MemoryObject to hardware capabilities and record findings in an ADR.
Resolve how capability unforgeability is preserved across machine boundaries (cryptographic capabilities, sturdy references, proxies).
AI action capabilities must be revocable by the user at any time (§7 revocation).
Capability safety layer: no object access without a typed capability (§7, §9).
Native isolation path step 3: attach an explicit capability set to the new Component at creation.
Study seL4 capability derivation trees, CSpaces, revocation and formal-verification approach for the CAP design.
Study CHERI capability hardware for ABI escape hatches and future hardware-enforced capabilities (cross-ref §8).
Study capability-oriented research OSes (KeyKOS, EROS, CapROS, Capsicum, Barrelfish, Theseus) for capability persistence, revocation and confinement patterns.
Create capabilities: mint, derive (attenuate), transfer across a channel, and revoke.
Native Platform layer: Capabilities.
Linux-derived kernel: capability enforcement in the kernel.
